articles.summary: The forty-hour workweek, a staple of modern business, has been a subject of debate for decades. Despite being written into law in 1938, the core concept of a 40-hour workweek has remained largely unchanged. The Bureau of Economic Analysis reports that the average American worker now produces 16 hours of output for every 40 hours of work, a significant increase from the 1970s. This phenomenon is attributed to the rise of machines and automation, which have freed up time for workers to pursue other activities. The article argues that this shift in the way work is organized is not a natural progression, but rather an arrangement that has been maintained for so long that it has become a standard of the modern economy.

articles.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
articles.summary: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG is achieved through the use of maximum inner product search with learned support functions, a technique that trains small neural networks to route queries toward their best match faster. This approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time. By leveraging the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search, this method can be particularly effective in applications where queries arise from short user-generated questions and keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text.
